title: AWS shared responsibility model
learningObjective: Describe AWS's responsibilities, the customer's responsibilities, shared controls, and how the split changes between EC2, RDS, Lambda and S3.
foundation: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud: the hardware, software, networking and facilities that run AWS services.
You are responsible for security IN the cloud: your data, who can access it, and how you configure services.
The more managed the service, the more AWS takes on. With EC2 you patch the operating system; with RDS and Lambda, AWS does.
engineer: AWS: physical security of data centers, hardware, global network, hypervisor and the software that runs managed services.
Customer: customer data, platform/application/identity and access management, OS/network/firewall configuration (for EC2), client-side and server-side encryption choices, network traffic protection.
Shared controls: patch management (AWS patches infrastructure, customer patches guest OS/apps), configuration management, awareness and training (AWS trains its staff, customers train theirs).

By service: EC2 (IaaS): customer manages guest OS, apps, security groups and data. RDS: AWS manages OS and database engine patching, backups infrastructure; customer manages database users, network access, data and encryption settings. Lambda: AWS manages runtime and OS; customer manages code, permissions and data. S3: customer manages bucket policies, Block Public Access, encryption options and data.

example.title: Same app, different split
body: On EC2, the team patches Amazon Linux monthly. After moving the database to RDS, AWS patches the database engine during the maintenance window, but the team still manages database users, security groups and encryption.

prerequisites: An AWS account (use an IAM Identity Center user, not root)
permissions: Read-only access to explore; least-privilege permissions to change resources
limits: Conceptual objective: explore in the console; no configuration limits are tested
portal: EC2 > Instances: you manage the OS (Systems Manager Patch Manager).
RDS > Maintenance window: AWS-managed engine patching.
S3 > Block Public Access settings: your responsibility.

misconceptions.myth: AWS is responsible for securing your data in S3.
misconceptions.reality: You control access and encryption choices.

misconceptions.myth: RDS customers patch the database engine.
misconceptions.reality: AWS does; customers set the maintenance window.

architectureDecisions: Prefer managed services to shift operational security tasks to AWS.

walkthrough.subtitle: Ask "who patches what?" for three services and watch the line between AWS and you move.
learn: Security OF the cloud vs IN the cloud
What the customer is responsible for
How the split shifts with EC2, RDS and Lambda

steps.label: Who patches?
steps.title: A server is hacked. Whose fault is it?
body: A company runs a web server on AWS. Attackers get in through an old, unpatched operating system.
Is that AWS's problem or the company's? The shared responsibility model answers this.

steps.label: AWS's side
steps.title: AWS: security OF the cloud
body: AWS protects the infrastructure that runs every service: the data centers, the hardware, the network, and the software that runs the services.
You can't visit or configure any of this, so AWS is responsible for it.

steps.label: Your side
steps.title: You: security IN the cloud
body: You are responsible for what you put in the cloud and how you configure it: your data, who has access (IAM), encryption choices, network and firewall settings, and on EC2 the guest operating system and your apps.

callout.text: If you can configure it, you are usually responsible for configuring it securely.

steps.label: Shared
steps.title: Some controls are shared
body: Patch management: AWS patches the infrastructure; you patch your guest OS and apps. Configuration management: AWS configures its devices; you configure your OS, databases and apps.
Awareness and training: AWS trains its staff; you train yours.

steps.label: EC2
steps.title: Case 1: Amazon EC2 (most yours)
body: With EC2 you get a virtual server. AWS secures the host and the hypervisor. You patch the guest OS, install and update apps, configure security groups, and protect your data.
So the hacked server from step 1 is the customer's responsibility.

steps.label: RDS
steps.title: Case 2: Amazon RDS (shared)
body: With RDS, AWS also patches the database engine and the OS under it, and runs backups if you enable them.
You still manage database users and permissions, network access, encryption settings, and your data.

steps.label: Lambda
steps.title: Case 3: AWS Lambda (most AWS)
body: With Lambda there is no server for you to see. AWS runs the OS, the runtime and the scaling.
You are responsible for your function code, its IAM permissions, and the data it handles.

callout.text: The more managed the service, the more AWS takes on. But your data and access are always yours.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: The line moves, the rule doesn't
body: AWS secures the cloud itself; you secure what you put in it.
recap: AWS: facilities, hardware, network, managed service software
Shared: patching, configuration, training (each on its own layer)
EC2: you patch the guest OS
RDS: AWS patches the engine; you manage users and data
Lambda: you own code and permissions
